lines: In 2019, a typical home was affordable in 48 of the fifty states.
Today? 9.
In New York, the mortgage on a typical home would eat 55 percent of a family's income.
Every single month.
In Ohio, 24.
And the number two state isn't California.
It's a state with about twice as many cattle as people.
We ranked all fifty states with official numbers.
Stay to the end, and you'll see exactly where yours lands.
Lenders have an old rule of thumb.
Your housing payment shouldn't be more than twenty eight percent of what you earn before taxes.
Go above it, and a home stops being a home. It becomes a stretch.
So we tested every state against it.
The typical home listed for sale in each state over the last twelve months, from Realtor dot com.
The typical household income, from the Census Bureau.
Ten percent down, and a thirty year fixed mortgage at today's average rate, 7.24 percent, from Freddie Mac.
And we didn't even count property taxes or insurance.
The real numbers are higher than everything you're about to see.
First, the whole country.
This is the mortgage on a typical American home, as a share of a typical income, every month since 2016.
The dashed line is the twenty eight percent rule.
In January 2021, rates were under three percent, and a typical home took about eighteen percent of income.
Easy.
Then rates more than doubled. By October 2023, the same math hit thirty eight percent.
Today it's around 34.
The country as a whole is over the line. But the country is an average.
Your state isn't.
Part one. Where a house still makes sense.
Only 9 states still pass the twenty eight percent test.
Almost all of them are in the Midwest.
Indiana, at number forty one, misses the line by half a point.
Number fifty. The most affordable state for a home in America.
Ohio.
A typical listed home in Ohio costs about 281 thousand dollars.
Less than half of California.
With a typical household income of 85 thousand, the mortgage takes 24 percent.
Comfortably under the line.
Number forty nine is the surprise.
Illinois.
Chicago is the third biggest city in America.
And Illinois still has some of the most affordable homes in the country. 24 percent of income.
Nebraska, Iowa, Kansas and Missouri follow, all around twenty five percent.
And Maryland is the odd one out.
Homes there aren't cheap, at 424 thousand dollars.
But Maryland has one of the highest household incomes in America, so it still squeaks under the line.
Part two. Over the line.
From forty down to twenty one, the share climbs from 29 percent to 38.
Every one of these states fails the rule today.
In 2019, every one of them passed.
Texas lands at thirty six.
Texas homes are cheaper than people think, around 357 thousand dollars.
And incomes are around the national typical. 31 percent.
Over the line, but not by much.
Now look at Mississippi. Number twenty.
It has some of the cheapest homes in the country, around 296 thousand dollars.
But it also has the lowest household income in the country.
So even a cheap home takes 38 percent.
Cheap is relative.
Part three. The breaking point.
From twenty to eleven, a typical home takes around forty percent of income.
Florida, Arizona, Nevada, Colorado, Utah, Washington and Tennessee are all in here.
Florida is number seventeen.
For years, Florida was where people went to make their money go further.
No state income tax, and homes cheaper than the Northeast.
Today a typical listed home there costs about 422 thousand dollars, and the mortgage takes 40 percent of income.
Before insurance, which in Florida is a story of its own.

Number ten, Wyoming. 43 percent.
Number nine, Rhode Island.

Number seven, Oregon.
Number six, Massachusetts. Homes cost 734 thousand dollars.

Number five, Idaho. 49 percent. Almost half of every paycheck.
Number four, Hawaii, at 52.
And number three, California, at 53.
Number two.
Montana.
Montana has about one point one million people. And around twice as many cattle.
But a typical home listed in Montana now costs about 629 thousand dollars.
And the typical household earns around 87 thousand.
The mortgage would take 53 percent of income. A hair above California.
And number one. The hardest state in America to afford a typical home.
New York.
A typical listed home: about 654 thousand dollars.
A typical household income: about 87 thousand.
At today's rate, the mortgage alone is about 4,014 dollars a month.
55 percent of income. Twice what the rule allows.
So how much would you need to earn to pass the rule?
In New York, about 172 thousand dollars a year. Twice what the typical household makes.
In Ohio? About 74 thousand. Less than the typical Ohio household already earns.
Part four. What changed.
Here's every state, then and now. Across the bottom, 2019. Up the side, today.
In 2019, only California and Hawaii were over the line. Everyone else was fine.
Since then, Wyoming went from 16 percent to 43.
Montana, from 24 to 53. Idaho, from 22 to 49.
The states that got hit hardest weren't the expensive coasts.
Many were the cheap, quiet states people moved to when they could work from anywhere.
Prices went up there. Incomes didn't keep up. And then rates doubled.
So what would fix it? We reran every state at lower rates.
At today's rate, 9 states pass. At six percent, 17.
At five, 25. At four percent, 34.
And at three percent, where rates were in 2021, 44 states would pass again.
But even at zero percent interest, a typical New York home would still take 23 percent of income.
In some places, the rate isn't the problem. The price is.
One honest caveat.
We used listing prices, not final sale prices, and listings in places like Montana include a lot of high end homes.
The ranking at the top holds either way.
So in 2019, 48 states passed the test. Today, 9 do.
And the last state standing?
Ohio. Where a typical home still costs less than a quarter of a paycheck.
